label: GPT-6.1 Terra
output:
Dear Nana,

I keep trying to write this and getting stuck, so I’m just going to start by saying I love you. I wish I could be there with you and Denise tonight, sitting in the kitchen on Kathleen Street, probably getting in the way while you both tell me there’s nothing left to do.

I’m sorry I can’t be there for the move. I’m on call all week, and I really did try to find someone to swap with me. I know you’d tell me not to make a fuss, and everyone keeps saying it’s fine, but I still feel guilty. You’ve been there for me so many times, and I wanted to be there for you tomorrow. I’m glad Denise is with you, though, and I’m glad she can read this to you for me.

Fifty-one years in that house. I’m trying to imagine how many cups of tea that works out to, and I don’t think even I could build a computer big enough to count them. How many dinners, how many people through the door, how many times somebody ended up in that kitchen needing food or advice or both.

When I think about the house, I usually think about summer. I’d get to stay with you, and everything felt a little slower. You let me stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays on that little kitchen TV, as long as I dried the dishes. At the time I thought I’d negotiated a pretty good deal: stay up late and watch baseball, with only a small amount of work involved. Looking back, you probably had a pretty good deal too. You got the dishes dried and a kid who was happy to stand there doing them.

I also think about the back steps. You’d be out there at six in the morning with your tea, and sometimes I’d come out and sit with you. You never talked until you’d finished your cup. I loved that, even when I was too young to know why. There was no need to fill the quiet or ask what we were going to do that day. We could just sit there. I still think about those mornings when things get loud and busy down here.

And then there was crib, which was considerably less peaceful.

You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. I’d like Denise to pause here so you have a chance to defend yourself, although I don’t think there’s much of a defence. You were playing a child.

But I’m glad you didn’t let me win. You taught me how to count my hand, how to pay attention, and how to lose without throwing the board across the room. At least, I hope I learned that last part. And when I finally skunked you at fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still remember how proud I felt. It was a real win, and you made a real celebration out of it. I’m not sure I’ve ever been rewarded so generously for beating someone at anything since.

I love that you still play on Tuesdays with the church ladies. Eighty-eight years old and still keeping your skills sharp. When I heard Elmwood has a crib league, I thought, well, they have no idea what’s coming. Please give them a little time to settle in before you start collecting butter tarts.

There are so many things from that house I’ll carry with me. Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I asked for the crib board. I’m happy those things are staying in the family. But what I really love about the house isn’t something we can pack. It’s the way it felt to be there with you. You raised half the family in that kitchen, or at least it seems that way to me, and you made room for all of us. The house has always felt like you to me: welcoming, warm, and perfectly capable of putting someone to work drying dishes.

I think about Grandpa Walt there too. He’s part of those memories, and I know leaving the house after all those years together must bring a lot back. I miss him. I’m grateful for all the time we had there with both of you, and I know those memories don’t stay behind just because someone else will eventually have the keys.

You’ve always looked after me, even from a distance. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a card with a twenty-dollar bill taped inside and wrote, “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I still laugh about that. I was a grown adult with a job, and you were making sure I had pizza money because of how I looked on a screen. It was such a Nana thing to do. You found a way to take care of me from Sudbury, and you made me laugh while you were at it.

And last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner, you asked if the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. Now every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?” I love that you ask. For the record, sometimes things do break, and sometimes I even fix them. I’m hoping that by the time you hear this, the internet has had the good manners to stay in one piece.

I want you to know how proud I am of you. You chose Elmwood Terrace yourself. Nobody made you do it, and I know that doesn’t mean it’s easy to leave a place you’ve called home for 51 years. It takes a lot to make a change like this, even when it’s one you want. It’s okay to be excited and sad about it at the same time. I probably am, and I’m not even the one moving.

Elmwood looks nice, Nana. You’ve got the room on the second floor, with the big maple outside and a view of the parking lot. I figure the maple will be lovely, and the parking lot will give you a chance to keep an eye on everybody’s driving. Between that and the crib league, you’ll have plenty to keep you busy.

I hope tonight you and Denise can sit for a while and enjoy that kitchen without worrying too much about tomorrow. Have a cup of tea, tell each other a story or two, and maybe give the dishes one last chance to dry themselves. I wish I were at the table with you. But I’m there in all those summers, all those games, and every quiet morning on the back steps. Thank you for making that house such a wonderful place to come home to.

I’ll be up the weekend of December 5, once my rotation is done. We’ll play the first game at the new place on the crib board. I’ll be practising until then, so don’t expect me to let you win.

Love you always.
